content: Premature birth, also referred to as preterm birth, occurs when a baby is delivered before the standard duration of pregnancy is completed. In most cases, this is defined as childbirth occurring before 37 completed weeks of gestation, calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP). Conversely, postmature birth is defined as delivery occurring after 42 weeks of gestation. The typical length of human gestation is 266 days, but for practical purposes, it is often calculated as 280 days or 40 weeks from the LMP, assuming conception occurs approximately 14 days after the LMP. In the United States, approximately 12% of babies, or 1 in 8, are born prematurely each year. Globally, determining rates of prematurity is more challenging due to limited access to professional obstetric care in developing regions, which makes accurate assessment of gestational age less reliable. In less developed regions, it is estimated that 5% of births in 2000 were premature, with one-third of low birth weight deliveries attributed to preterm birth. The shorter the duration of pregnancy, the higher the risk of complications. Premature infants face an increased risk of mortality within the first year of life, with the majority of deaths occurring in the neonatal period (the first month of life). Worldwide, prematurity accounts for 10% of neonatal deaths, equating to approximately 500,000 deaths annually. In developed countries like the United States, where infections and other causes of neonatal death have been significantly reduced, prematurity is the leading cause of neonatal mortality, responsible for 25% of such deaths. Premature infants are also at heightened risk for developing severe health issues, including cerebral palsy, chronic lung disease, gastrointestinal problems, intellectual disabilities, and vision or hearing impairments. Additionally, they are more susceptible to experiencing depression during adolescence. Despite the identification of several risk factors for prematurity, nearly half of all preterm births occur without a known cause. When conditions allow, medical professionals may attempt to halt premature labor to extend the pregnancy to full term, thereby improving the baby’s chances of survival and health. However, there is currently no reliable method to prevent or stop preterm labor in all cases. Alarmingly, the rate of preterm births in the United States has increased by 30% over the past two decades. In developed countries, premature infants are typically cared for in Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs). Neonatologists, specialists in the care of critically ill or premature infants, oversee their treatment. In the NICU, premature babies are placed under radiant warmers or in incubators (also known as isolettes), which are climate-controlled bassinets designed to maintain warmth and minimize exposure to germs. Modern neonatal intensive care involves advanced monitoring of temperature, respiration, cardiac function, oxygenation, and brain activity. Treatments may include intravenous fluids and nutrition, oxygen supplementation, mechanical ventilation, and medications. In developing countries, where advanced medical equipment and even reliable electricity may be unavailable, simple interventions such as kangaroo care (skin-to-skin warming), promoting breastfeeding, and basic infection control measures can significantly reduce preterm morbidity and mortality. The term ex-premies is used to describe preterm infants who were born before the standard 37 weeks of gestation.
